newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ILO chief says will push for global labour rights.
newsitem.headline: ILO chief says will push for global labour rights.

text.p: International Labour Organisation (ILO) Director-General Michel Hansenne said on Wednesday he was launching a major drive to ensure all member countries around the globe observed basic worker rights.

And he told a news conference that both emerging and advanced economies who held back were bound to face growing trade boycotts and campaigns against their goods by consumer groups and other non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

"We are going to step up our drive to have all ILO members to ratify our basic core conventions," said Hansenne, whose 78-year-old organisation now includes 174 states. He would be working for a formal declaration from all members by next year.

"Now this dossier has been formally consigned to us by the international community, we intend to take it seriously," Hansenne added. The ILO would be seeking wider rights to monitor observance of basic codes.

He said countries which had stoutly resisted having the World Trade Organisation (WTO) work on trade-and-labour rules and had insisted the issue should only be handled in the ILO should now prove their sincerity.

"They have committed themselves in the WTO Ministerial Declaration issued in Singapore last month to working in the ILO to ensure basic labour codes are observed. Now they must show this was not just words," Hansenne declared.
The ILO's core codes cover forced labour, freedom to belong to a union, the right to organise unions, child labour, equal pay for men and women, and non-discrimination in employment.

After years of fierce debate, WTO trade ministers agreed in Singapore that the labour issue should be dealt with in the Geneva-based ILO and should not be used as an excuse for protectionist action against goods from cheap-labour countries.

The United States, France and some other industrialised powers, where workers fear jobs are draining away to developing countries where work standards and salaries are lower, wanted the WTO to work for a trade-and-labour link.
This would have allowed for trade sanctions against states found by WTO dispute panels to be violating the ILO codes.

Hansenne, who had a tentative invitation to speak in Singapore withdrawn after procedural objections from some developing countries, said he took the ministers' decision to mean that his organisation should now work hard on the issue.

Countries like Malaysia, which had insisted that the ILO and not the WTO was the right forum for the debate and should be "given teeth" to promote labour rights, "have the ball in their court," he added. "We must now get the teeth," he said.

Hansenne, former Belgian social affairs minister, said he had been warning developing countries that in the longer term they would inevitably face mounting trade problems if their labour practices were seen as violating basic standards.

"Public opinion will become increasingly important over the next few years. The sanction of the market will be more important than any government or international sanctions," he added, pointing to several recent consumer boycotts.

A growing number of multinational companies with subsidiaries in developing countries were asking the ILO to help them demonstrate that they were not exploiting workers and boosting profits by paying low wages, he said.

Another example of the growing global interest in labour issues was the fierce reaction among international trade union bodies to South Korea's new labour laws and its refusal to grant immediate recognition of a major labour grouping, he added.
